title: A 39-year-old woman with transient convulsions and vision disturbances: a case report
case_prompt:
A 39-year-old Chinese woman was admitted to the intensive care unit with acute pancreatitis after presenting three hours earlier with sudden abdominal pain. Three hours after admission, she had a brief generalized convulsion lasting approximately 10 seconds that resolved spontaneously. Fifteen minutes later, she reported complete loss of vision in both eyes. An ophthalmologic examination revealed no abnormalities.

Her history was notable for two prior episodes of pancreatitis. She also had untreated hypertension and hyperlipidemia, and a history of anxiety treated intermittently with propranolol, alprazolam, and long-term venlafaxine. She denied other systemic, infectious, or psychiatric illnesses.

On examination, her blood pressure was 145/77 mmHg, and other vital signs were within normal limits. She was alert and oriented. Pupils were equal, 3 mm in diameter, and reactive to light, but she was unable to see objects or count fingers at 30 cm, although she could perceive light. Optokinetic nystagmus was absent, and fundoscopic examination was normal. Neurologic examination of cranial nerves, motor and sensory function, reflexes, and coordination was unremarkable. There were no meningeal signs.

Laboratory studies on admission showed a normal complete blood count except for a neutrophil count of 8.68×10^9/L (normal 2–7.71). Liver function tests, procalcitonin, D-dimer, immunologic and thyroid panels were normal. Hepatitis A, B, and C serologies, syphilis, and HIV tests were negative. Lipid profile revealed severe hypertriglyceridemia (78.68 mmol/L; normal 0.34–2.30) and elevated total cholesterol (10.62 mmol/L; normal 3.9–6.46). Electrolytes showed K^+ 3.03 mmol/L, Mg^2+ 0.67 mmol/L, Ca^2+ 1.76 mmol/L, and CRP 277 mg/L (normal 0–5.0). Renal function and serum amylase were normal on admission; on day 2, creatinine rose to 105.5 µmol/L (normal 41.0–73.0) and amylase to 466 U/L (normal 0–150).

Abdominal CT on admission confirmed pancreatic swelling. Given the acute cortical blindness, a noncontrast head CT and head and neck CT angiography were performed, showing no intracranial hemorrhage, arterial occlusion, or vascular malformation. After excluding hemorrhage, she received intravenous thrombolysis with recombinant tissue plasminogen activator. Three hours later, a brain MRI demonstrated no apparent abnormality.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Considered hysterical blindness or visual agnosia — “For patients with hysterical blindness and visual agnosia, the blinking reflex and the optokinetic nystagmus exist. However, in our patient, when the examiner suddenly illuminated the patient’s eye with a strong beam, the patient had no blink reflex.”  
2. Considered acute ischemic stroke from bilateral PCA infarction — “Considering that acute ischemic stroke is the most common cause of cortical blindness… Intravenous thrombolysis was done… However, the patient’s visual disturbances did not recover after intravenous thrombolysis, and 3 hours after intravenous thrombolysis, the patient underwent a brain MRI, which showed no apparent abnormality.”  
3. Considered epilepsy as cause of visual disturbance — “Before visual disturbances, the patient had transient convulsions; therefore, epilepsy should be the differential diagnosis.” Excluded by lack of further seizures and non-epileptiform EEG — “3 days after admission, the electroencephalogram (EEG) showed medium–high amplitude θ waves… She has had no convulsion since her first transient convulsions.”  
4. Considered neuromyelitis optica — “Neuromyelitis optica (NMO) also presents with initial sudden visual disturbances with intraorbital pain. In addition, the fundus examination of the patient with NMO revealed papilledema and serum aquaporin-4 antibody (AQP4) positivity.” Excluded by normal fundoscopic exam and negative AQP4 — “Optokinetic nystagmus was absent, and fundoscopic examination was normal.” and “Only human coronavirus HKU1 was found positive in this patient.”  
5. Considered intracranial infection or autoimmune encephalitis — “Intracranial infection and AE can also cause visual impairment.” Excluded by negative CSF metagenomic and antibody testing — “AQP4 antibodies, AE antibodies, and CSF full set of pathogenic microorganisms metagenomic testing results came back… Only human coronavirus HKU1 was found positive.”  
6. Considered venous sinus thrombosis and AV malformation — “It is worth mentioning that transient convulsion and visual disturbances can also occur in patients with PRES and intracranial venous sinus thrombosis.” Excluded by normal venous flow on MRV and DSA — “the superior sagittal, bilateral sigmoid, and bilateral transverse sinuses were poorly visualized, the venous returns are fine.”  
7. Considered other causes (PML, Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, porphyria, mitochondrial encephalopathy, lead poisoning, methanol poisoning, carbon monoxide poisoning, migraine) — “In addition to epilepsy, NMO, intracranial infection, AE, and PRES, the broad differential diagnosis included PML, Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, porphyria, mitochondrial encephalopathy, lead poisoning, methanol poisoning, carbon monoxide poisoning, and migraine.”
